item.title: Newsom's death penalty gamble could help him in 2028 — or come back to bite him
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A view of the East Block of San Quentin Rehab Center's death row, which was shut down by Gov. Gavin Newsom earlier in his term before he announced Thursday that he was commuting the sentences of condemned inmates. (Robert Gauthier / Los Angeles Times) While running for California governor in 2018, Gavin Newsom declared that he would rather be bold and fail than retreat to the safety of mediocrity. The two-term governor known for taking big political risks once again made good on that vow Thursday when he moved to offer clemency to every inmate sentenced to death in California. Amid a hum of speculation about how the mass commutation could help or hurt his presidential prospects in 2028, the Democratic politician sent a clear, defining message to Americans about where he stands and the type of leader they could expect. “If my job is just to read the polls, you can have an AI chatbot as governor,” Newsom said in an interview Friday. “I was hired for my judgment, and like it or hate it, that was why I think I was given this privilege, and that’s the responsibility of a leader. My job’s leadership, not stewardship. It’s not management. It’s to lead. “I’m here to change polls, change minds.” The sweeping decision comes more than 20 years after Newsom emerged in the national consciousness when, as mayor of San Francisco, he defied federal law and allowed same-sex marriages in the City by the Bay. California Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks at the "Stop the Power Grab rally" at the Hollywood Palladium in Los Angeles on Nov. 1, 2026. (Ariana Drehsler / For The Times) Bold moves that test the limits of his power, such as a controversial, first-in-the-nation stay-at-home order during the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic and spearheading Proposition 50 last year to redraw California’s congressional districts to offset Republican attempts to gerrymander red states, have defined his leadership, for good or bad. The Democratic governor said those kinds of decisions are “sort of embedded in my DNA.” About a decade ago he said he was pushed to describe his core motivation. Though he admits it sounds trite, the governor said: “It’s to stand up for ideals and strike out against injustice.” The death penalty, he said, is not handed out equally. He quoted Bryan Stevenson, the founder of Equal Justice Initiative, who said you’re better off being rich and guilty than poor and innocent. “I couldn’t not have done this,” Newsom said. “There was an easy out, but ... I would the rest of my life felt, you know, ashamed of myself.” Commuting the death sentences of all 548 state prisoners awaiting execution pushes the bounds of his authority once again. California voters have twice rejected ballot measures to abolish the death penalty , first in 2012 and again in 2016, and Newsom’s decision overrides the will of the courts and state laws that permit capital punishment. Read more: Newsom moves to commute all California death sentences to life in prison without parole Under the state Constitution, Newsom has the power to commute about 40% of the death sentences on his own. The rest of the cases, which involve prisoners who had a felony conviction on their record prior to receiving a death sentence, or racked up additional crimes while awaiting execution, require approval from the California Supreme Court — a constitutional check to ensure the governor’s actions are not an abuse of power. The court rejected 10 commutations handed out by Gov. Jerry Brown in his last full month in office — all of which involved people convicted of multiple felonies — and did not provide an explanation for the action. Despite Newsom’s push to commute all death sentences, capital punishment remains legal in California and prosecutors can continue seeking that punishment. Los Angeles County Dist. Atty. Nathan Hochman speaks during a news conference at the Hall of Justice last month. (Ronaldo Bolaños / Los Angeles Times) Los Angeles County Dist. Atty. Nathan Hochman said until the law is changed, his office “will continue to evaluate every death penalty-eligible case with the rigor, care and restraint these decisions demand.” Sacramento County Sheriff Jim Cooper urged Newsom to reconsider the commutations. He said he remembers watching Luis Bracamontes, who was sentenced to death for killing Sacramento County Sheriff’s Deputy Danny Oliver and Placer County Sheriff’s Detective Michael Davis Jr. in 2014, “laugh in court while their families, including Danny’s two young daughters, had to sit and watch. “Deputy Danny Oliver and Detective Michael Davis Jr. should be alive today, enjoying long and healthy lives with their families,” Cooper said in a statement. “Instead, the man who murdered them has now escaped his sentence.” Others accused the governor of reducing the death penalty sentences to seek an advantage in the 2028 presidential election. “The people of California deserve leaders who put politics and personal ambition aside and pursue truth, accountability, and justice with courage, integrity, and transparency,” said Michael Hestrin, Riverside County district attorney, in a statement. “Instead they have been presented with a decision that demonstrates a profound disregard for the victims, their families, and the prosecutors who dedicated themselves to seeking justice on their behalf.” Luis Bracamontes looks up in Sacramento Superior Court in 2018 as the verdict is read in the killing of two law enforcement officers. Bracamontes was found guilty. (Rich Pedroncelli / Associated Press) A poll conducted in August by the Pew Research Center found that about two-thirds of voters nationally favor the death penalty for people convicted of murder. Political analysts suggest that reducing the sentences adds to Newsom’s credentials as a progressive leader and aligns him with Democratic primary voters on the issue if he runs for president. Republicans, however, could take advantage of Newsom’s action and cast him as a soft-on-crime liberal who is out of touch with most Americans, which risks turning away moderate voters. But others cautioned that national political elections are hard to predict. Gar Culbert, chair of the political science department at Cal State Los Angeles, said it would be politically advantageous for Newsom to try to appeal to the Democratic Party’s base as he considers a run for president. Culbert said he doesn’t believe the death penalty will be a substantial issue in a general election when, if Newsom becomes the Democratic presidential nominee, his Republican challenger would attack his record as California governor regardless. “It’s possible he’s not being strategic,” Culbert said. “Maybe he doesn’t have to be strategic because he just might think it’s the right thing to do.” The governor first issued a moratorium on executions about two months after he took office in 2019, saying capital punishment is discriminatory and unjust. Without the moratorium, 45 people would be subject to execution now, according to his office. Daniel Zingale worked for Newsom as a senior advisor in the governor’s office at the start of his first term. Part of Zingale’s job at the time was to consider how the governor’s actions would be received by the public. “The only piece of data he was not interested in in that process were the polls,” Zingale said. “His view, and I agree with this, is this is not an issue that you can leverage politically.” Read more: Gov. Gavin Newsom to block California death row executions, close San Quentin execution chamber Newsom’s decision to commute the sentences won’t have much practical effect in a state that has not executed a prisoner since 2006. At Newsom’s command, the death chamber was dismantled at San Quentin State Prison, now San Quentin Rehabilitation Center, after he issued his moratorium. His successor, Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra, has also said he will continue the pause on executions. There was no immediate need to offer commutations to save the lives of the inmates. Taking no action would have been the safe bet, Newsom said in an interview about his decision a day after he made the announcement. Many people around him, he said, advised him to do nothing. He also understands that commuting the sentences could make him vulnerable if he runs for president. “I’m not an idiot. The ads write themselves,” Newsom said. “But I just also would be fake. I wouldn’t be myself and if I’m going to be up there and not be myself, I couldn’t do that.” With the clock ticking on his time in office, the governor said he also doesn’t want to leave with regrets. “I don’t want to be one of the elders on some panel talking about what I would have, could have, should have done,” Newsom said. “I’ve spent my life trying not to be that person. I’ve been willing to take risks. I’ve been willing to go first on so many issues. “If others aren’t willing to do it, you know what? I’ll raise my hand, and I’m happy, honestly, to take the hits.” Sign up for Essential California for news, features and recommendations from the L.A. Times and beyond in your inbox six days a week. This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times . This article originally appeared on LA Times at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/death-sentence-clemency-newsom-takes-032948182.html

item.title: Trump picks Stephen Miller as chief of staff, signaling intent to stay the course
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Bo Erickson, Nandita Bose, Steve Holland and Trevor Hunnicutt WASHINGTON, Nov 6 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump named longtime aide Stephen Miller as his chief of staff on Friday, giving the architect of some of his toughest domestic policies one of the most powerful jobs in Washington after Republicans lost control of Congress. Miller, who will replace Susie Wiles, assumes the role as the president prepares to confront ‌a Democratic-led House of Representatives and Senate and a wave of congressional investigations into his administration. A longtime proponent of expansive presidential authority, Miller takes over at a moment when the Republican Party's defeat in Tuesday's ‌midterm elections could leave Trump more reliant on executive power to advance his domestic agenda. In a social media post, Trump called Miller "one of my most trusted advisors," and praised Wiles for doing "an outstanding job." Trump said the change would take effect on Monday. A White House official said Miller's appointment signals ​that Trump has no intention of rethinking his policies and instead is rewarding his most loyal aides. "He's not changing course," the official said, despite tens of millions of American voters repudiating Trump's domestic agenda and foreign policy. Trump said this week he was willing to work with Democrats on Capitol Hill. But elevating Miller, who is known for being caustic and uncompromising, could signal a more confrontational approach and a renewed push to advance the president's agenda on immigration and other issues, several White House officials said. Trump had been displeased with his political and communications operations in the run-up to Tuesday's election as his public approval ratings fell near record lows. This week, he said the White House needed to be "more aggressive" as Democrats retake congressional power, ‌according to a person briefed on the matter. "The mission now is more clear than ⁠ever," Miller said on X after his appointment. "Fight with all of our soul to support our President and defend this magnificent Republic." Hakeem Jeffries, who is set to become the new Democratic speaker of the House, responded to the announcement by calling Miller a "reckless extremist" in a posting on X. MILLER DRIVING IMMIGRATION CRACKDOWN Miller, 41, is one of Trump's longest-serving aides and one of ⁠only a few who served throughout his first and second terms in office. Since Trump's return to the White House in 2025, Miller has officially served as deputy chief of staff under Wiles, but he has wielded outsize influence across much of Trump's domestic agenda and has had the president's ear. He is perhaps best known for driving Trump's aggressive immigration crackdown, setting a goal of 3,000 arrests a day. The efforts to meet that target pushed masked US immigration officers into communities around the country, increasingly arresting people with no criminal ​records ​and who had been living in the country for decades. The crackdown, however, gets poor marks with Americans. Just 36% of respondents to ​a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed early this week approve of it, with 54% disapproving. Representative Robert Garcia, ‌the top Democrat on the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, said the party planned to investigate Miller's immigration policies. "Stephen Miller should lawyer up," he said. Miller was also deeply involved in Trump's campaign to remake the federal bureaucracy, which led to the dismissal of tens of thousands of civil servants in 2025. He was also a driving force behind the administration's battles with universities, diversity programs and other institutions. HAWKISH FOREIGN POLICY On foreign policy, Miller has been a vocal supporter of Trump's deadly military strikes on boats suspected of carrying drugs in the Caribbean and Pacific, a campaign that has raised legal questions. He has also praised US and Israeli strikes in Iran and defended a naval blockade and sanctions as ways to weaken Tehran and curb its ability to threaten its neighbors. It is not clear whether that is still his view after voters punished Republicans this week in part for the economic fallout from the Iran war. Marc Short, who was chief ‌of staff to then-Vice President Mike Pence in Trump's first term, said that in Miller, Trump is "getting someone who is wed to him" ​and who is willing to battle Congress over issues like immigration and congressional investigations. "It would not suggest that there is high expectation for bipartisan ​legislation," Short said in an interview. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, who faces Democratic calls for impeachment over the ​Iran war, celebrated Miller's promotion with a social media post reading, "Patriots in control," reflecting the enthusiasm of some Trump allies for putting Miller in a position of greater authority. SHAKE UP AFTER ELECTION ‌SETBACK The chief of staff typically wields great influence as the president's gatekeeper. The person ​manages White House staff, organizes the president's time and schedule, and ​oversees other government departments and lawmakers. Wiles, 69, who submitted her resignation on Thursday night, will move to Trump's political operation, according to a White House official. The veteran political operative from Florida was the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff. She brought decades of political experience to the role and was regarded as running a more disciplined operation than some of Trump's prior top aides. She maintained her role even ​while undergoing treatment earlier this year for early-stage breast cancer. Wiles rarely challenged Trump's policies ‌but brought discipline to an often chaotic operation and was seen as a voice of reason. Her exit raises questions about who will play her role. Trump ran through four chiefs of staff – an unusually ​high number – during his 2017-2021 term, as they were seen to have struggled to rein in the unpredictable president. (Reporting by Bo Erickson, Nandita Bose, Steve Holland, Jacob Bogage in Washington; Additional reporting by ​Bhargav Acharya and Susan Heavey; Writing by Trevor Hunnicutt; editing by Scott Malone, Colleen Jenkins, Ross Colvin and Jonathan Spicer) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/trump-promotes-stephen-miller-post-190429829.html

item.title: GOP's losses will raise pressure on conservative Supreme Court justices to retire
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The GOP’s sweeping losses in the midterm elections Tuesday set up an unsettling possibility for the party: If it doesn’t act now to confirm a new Supreme Court justice, it may not have another chance for years to come. That prospect is likely to ramp up pressure on the court’s two oldest conservatives - Justices Samuel A. Alito Jr., 76, and Clarence Thomas, 78 - to retire during the lame-duck period, while Republicans still have the votes to get a nominee confirmed by the Senate. The new Senate, in which Democrats will hold a majority, is seated on Jan. 3. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Alito, who joined the court in 2006, said last month he has no plans to retire during the lame-duck session. Thomas has said in the past he has no plans to step down from the court. He joined the court in 1991 and could become the longest-serving justice in its history in 2028. But given the magnitude of Democratic inroads in the Senate, legal and political experts said it could be 2033 before Republicans have a realistic shot at winning back enough seats in that chamber to approve a conservative justice. At that point, Alito and Thomas would be well into their 80s. Neither responded to a request for comment. “I think both have been making an implicit bet that they will live long enough … so that a Republican president can replace them with someone ideologically similar,” said Ed Whelan, a conservative attorney and senior fellow at the Ethics and Public Policy Center. This is likely to make many Republicans antsy, particularly those mindful of the lesson of Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, who died while still on the bench at 87, in September 2020. The liberal justice’s death allowed Republicans to move the court in a more conservative direction when they confirmed Justice Amy Coney Barrett to replace her weeks later. President Donald Trump nominated Barrett to replace Ginsburg, and over the vociferous objections of Democrats, Senate Republicans quickly muscled the nomination through just ahead of the 2020 presidential election. Trump remade the court with three picks in his first term - Barrett, Neil M. Gorsuch and Brett M. Kavanaugh - who pushed the court sharply to the right. The Supreme Court’s conservative 6-3 supermajority has delivered historic opinions on abortion, affirmative action, religious rights and much more that have thrilled Republicans. A younger replacement for Alito or Thomas could lock that advantage in for years to come. Liberals accused Republicans of hypocrisy for rapidly confirming Barrett after they blocked President Barack Obama’s nomination of Merrick Garland for 11 months in 2016, saying it was too close to the presidential election to confirm him. Trump won the White House, and Garland’s nomination was scuttled. Some observers think the window has already closed for Trump to nominate a fourth justice, which would allow him to leave a mark on the Supreme Court that few presidents have enjoyed. Republicans control 53 seats in the upper chamber, compared with 47 held by Democrats. But that split will shift to 52-48 as soon as Dec. 15, when Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) is seated as a result of a special election. A handful of moderate Senate Republicans like Maine’s Susan Collins and Alaska’s Lisa Murkowski might also have to be persuaded to back a Trump pick. The margin of error is thin enough that Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) posted Tuesday night on X that Trump probably won’t be able to get a suitable nominee confirmed. “Chance of confirming a worthy successor to Justice Thomas and/or Alito during President Trump’s term: Zero,” DeSantis wrote. “Chance of confirming a worthy successor during a hypothetical GOP admin 2029-2033: probably zero (GOP won’t be able to recapture enough seats in 28).” Harry Litman, a law professor at UCLA and a former U.S. attorney, said the optics of a justice retiring during the lame-duck session would also tarnish his or her reputation. “It would be the most crass and nakedly political resignation in the court’s history,” Litman said. Emily Hampsten, a spokeswoman for Sen. Dick Durbin (Illinois), the Democratic whip and a member of the Judiciary Committee, said a lame-duck nominee would create a backlash among voters and Democrats. “The American people will hold them accountable in 2028, and Democrats could justifiably refuse to confirm any Trump nominees for the next two years,” Hampsten said. That would curtail one of Trump’s other biggest legacies - the nomination of hundreds of lower court federal judges. Steve Vladeck, a Georgetown law professor, wrote on his blog that a lame-duck confirmation fight might also backfire on the GOP by building support for court reforms that Democrats are already eyeing during the next Congress. “The question would no longer be whether the Court deserves to be restructured, but whether the other side has left Democrats any choice,” Vladeck wrote. Gabe Roth, executive director of the reform group Fix the Court, said he thinks only small reforms will be possible while Trump is still president over the next two years. “Democrats would do well to focus on areas within the realm of court reform where there’s already strong bipartisan support,” Roth said. “That includes banning stock trading in the federal courts, adding more lower court judgeships to relieve ballooning caseloads, improving workplace conduct protections for judiciary staff and making access to court records free.” Speculation over whether Alito would retire flared over the summer when NPR published an erroneous account saying he was planning on stepping down. The story was later retracted. Alito said during a round of interviews to promote his new book last month that he had no plans to retire during the current term, which will end in June or July. The justice said he has more to contribute to the court but did consider whether to continue each term. “I intend to stick around through this term,” Alito said in the interview before the Supreme Court’s new term began last month. “I made that decision many months ago.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/11/05/gops-losses-will-raise-pressure-conservative-supreme-court-justices-retire/

item.title: Elizabeth Warren's new Senate role puts Wall Street and Trump on notice for hearings
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Democratic firebrand Elizabeth Warren, a consumer advocate known for her fierce battles over financial regulations, will take the gavel in January to become chair of the powerful Senate Banking Committee. According to a source familiar with her plans, the Massachusetts senator intends to use her expanded platform to advance legislation to tackle populist affordability issues with a focus on housing. The person familiar with her plans says Warren will use the committee's investigative powers to hold hearings and launch investigations into executive branch ethics and corporate practices, aiming to hold President Trump, the administration, Wall Street, and Big Tech accountable for economic decisions she views as having driven up costs for consumers. Warren is also expected to take steps to shield the Federal Reserve from White House overreach . Any future nominee for the Fed will have to go through her committee. Earlier this year, she rallied Democrats to oppose Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh's confirmation before the banking committee, stalling his eventual confirmation. Wall Street is likely to be another of Warren's targets. Before Republicans regained control of Congress, Democrats would have the chief executives of big banks testify before the Senate Banking and House Financial Services committees once a year. The banking industry can expect a return to that practice. Stephen Biggar, who covers the financial sector for Argus Research, says hearings will offer more transparency, but won't be accompanied by meaningful rulemaking. Biggar expects increased oversight, potentially more consumer protections, and actions to limit banks' market share size, such as blocking mergers. He added that there are concerns that the deregulation efforts and lower capital requirements for banks championed by Republicans are now at risk. James Angel, an associate professor at Georgetown University's McDonough School of Business, said he thinks the hearings will accomplish two things: producing information and sound bites that will get people to pay attention and galvanize public opinion. Second, Angel says they will serve as a deterrent for people in power. "If people will be held under oath and there's a prospect of perjury, that will deter people from doing 'Trumpier' things," Angel said in an interview. Angel also noted that any Trump appointee who has to be confirmed by Warren's committee will need to withstand bipartisan scrutiny and thus is more likely to be a moderate. Prediction markets, housing, AI, and credit card rates This summer, Warren teamed up with current Senate Banking Committee Chair Tim Scott to pass a sprawling bipartisan housing bill that addresses housing affordability by encouraging more homebuilding, expanding financing options, and restricting large corporate investors buying single-family homes. Warren is expected to continue her push to rein in private equity across industries that she sees jacking up costs for families. Warren also intends to conduct oversight into prediction markets and election betting platforms to prevent insider trading and platform manipulation. Before the midterm elections, Warren co-authored a letter with Utah Sen. John Curtis to executives of Kalshi and Polymarket asking them to explain how they would prevent candidates, campaign staff, and others with inside information from trading on election contracts. There are also potential areas of common ground with Republicans, including advancing bipartisan AI export-control bills. Warren worked on three such bills this year, including a measure to stop advanced AI chips from being used by China to develop dangerous systems. One area of agreement that could secure Trump's signature: capping credit card interest rates. It's something both Warren and Trump support, along with newly elected Democrats, including Texas's new senator, James Talarico. Follow Jennifer Schonberger on X @Jenniferisms and on Instagram . item.title: Vance faces a 2028 dilemma as Republicans question his ties to Trump
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The fight for the 2028 Republican primary is beginning to take shape on the heels of the GOP's devastating midterm losses, with Vice President Vance facing criticism for blaming the losses on the Iran war and other big-name Republicans appearing to stake out their own positions. The losses have created a huge opening for GOP White House hopefuls, including Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Sen. Ted Cruz (Texas), to go against Vance. It’s a fact seemingly recognized by Vance, who was quick to blame the Iran war for the historic drubbings, and Republicans at large. “The election results were bad news for every leader across the party, given the scale of the losses, but they were particularly tough for Vance’s 2028 prospects,” said Kevin Madden, the veteran Republican strategist who served as a senior adviser on Mitt Romney's 2012 presidential campaign. “Vance is now in the position of serving as a loyal vice president to a lame-duck president whose approval rating is in the 30’s and whose influence on the future of the party could be in question,” Madden added. Vance has long been seen as the front-runner to succeed President Trump as the GOP standard-bearer. A close second has been Secretary of State Marco Rubio. But questions are now being raised by Republicans over whether a candidate not directly tied to the administration would be stronger. “Tuesday made clear that the stink on Vice President Vance and Secretary [Marco] Rubio may be too much to overcome as the election was a referendum on the job they are doing,” said one top GOP operative who has spoken to DeSantis. “This certainly creates a lane for DeSantis, Cruz and others if they are willing to run in a potentially impossible year to win,” the operative added. In blaming the losses on Iran, Vance put some daylight between himself and his boss. Trump, for his part, has doubled down in insisting his administration made the right decision to start the war. “Vance’s profile as a candidate is directly tied to the Trump legacy. A candidate for 2028 without an ability to craft a more unique, independent profile of their own will face challenges in this next two-year cycle,” Madden predicted. The GOP operative who spoke to The Hill said 2028 “is going to be a difficult year for Republican presidential contenders if there aren’t substantial changes.” If there aren’t changes, the operative said DeSantis might wait until 2032 to run for president. DeSantis over the last 48 hours or so has certainly sounded like someone with the White House on his mind. The Florida governor, who unsuccessfully challenged Trump for the Republican nomination in 2024, was among the first this week to offer his own pointed view on what went wrong for GOP candidates, pointing to the war in Iran and high gas prices. In an interview with SiriusXM host Stephen A. Smith, he accused some in his party of “gaslighting” voters by not acknowledging their economic anxiety. DeSantis has also pointed out that the red wall in Florida, where the GOP won a Senate race and a gubernatorial contest, held. That’s an argument that would seem to point toward his leadership of the state. Republicans did lose three House races in districts that were redrawn to give GOP candidates an edge, and they are behind in a fourth. The gubernatorial and Senate races were also closer than expected. But DeSantis can certainly make an argument about his state being a GOP bastion. Cruz ahead of the elections had been more transparent about his ambition to run for president, saying he would entertain the idea of a 2028 run after the midterms. On his podcast, Cruz compared the losses to the drubbing Republicans took after Watergate, a comparison that would seem to at least raise the issue of corruption as being a factor in the GOP’s terrible night. He also criticized the Trump tariffs and the Iran war for raising costs. “Food is too high. Gas is too high. Diesel is too high. Insurance is too high. Life is too high,” he said. GOP strategists predict that after Tuesday’s results, their primary will be wide open. “Vance is completely unacceptable to any Republican who can accurately assess the reasons for the pasting we received on Tuesday,” one former Trump campaign aide said. “It not only opens the door for others, it should soundly shut the door for JD Vance.” Other Republicans say Tuesday’s results force Vance to stake his claim early or face the consequences of a more crowded field. “Vance needs to announce first with the president’s endorsement,” said Susan Del Percio, the veteran Republican strategist. “If he doesn’t do it in January, it’ll look like a sign of weakness and everyone will know the president isn’t on board. And that’s the million dollar question: Is he out of favor with the president?” One former Trump aide — who asked for anonymity to offer a candid assessment — said that right now, there’s “more space than less space” for other Republicans to enter the race. “Let’s face it, Cruz and DeSantis were the winners in our party the other night,” the former aide said. “This is absolutely the beginning of the end of the Trump era." The former aide added that Trump “is still going to be a potent force in the primary. If he endorses you, that’s 30 percent right off the bat." But the former aide predicted it would be difficult for Vance to keep his distance from Trump and that he would be pigeonholed to his stances. “Imagine, he’s going to have to answer to Trump’s whim or rant of the day every day,” the former aide said. “And he’s not going to stand in stark contrast to the president because Trump will shred him. “That’s just not an enviable place,” the former aide added. item.title: Democrats' midterm wins could change how we elect presidents by 2028
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Could this year's big blue midterm wave transform how America elects its next president? Now that Democrats have won complete control of governor's mansions and both legislative chambers in five battleground states — Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin, Nevada and Arizona — there is a chance that the Electoral College, as we know it, could soon become a thing of the past. That isn't speculation. In fact, the plan is already in motion. Over the last two decades, 18 states and Washington, D.C., have formally agreed to award all of their electoral votes to whichever presidential ticket wins the most votes nationwide, regardless of the outcome in their own state or district. Until now, this legal agreement — official name: the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact (NPVIC) — hasn't taken effect because the jurisdictions that have joined it only control 222 total electoral votes, which falls short of the 270 required to activate the compact (and elect a president). But what if you add Pennsylvania (19 electoral votes), Michigan (15), Arizona (11), Wisconsin (10) and Nevada (6) to the list? That gets you to 283 (assuming that all of them join and the compact survives potential constitutional challenges). Since Election Day, the Democratic shift in statehouses across the country has been overshadowed by the massive Democratic shift on Capitol Hill . But as the dust settles, attention is turning toward a new possibility: that a handful of states might suddenly have the power to ensure that whoever wins the national popular vote in 2028 will also win the presidency (which hasn't always been the case ). "The time is right," Carrie Rheingans, a Democrat in the Michigan House of Representatives, told the New York Times this week . "This blue tsunami is really going to help push this forward across the whole nation." "National popular vote will be something that we'll prioritize early in the session," added Kelda Roys, a Democratic state lawmaker in Wisconsin. Here's everything you need to know about the national popular vote compact — and its chances of taking effect. How does the Electoral College currently work? The Electoral College is a system of indirect democracy in which the winner of the U.S. presidential election is determined not by the combined number of votes a candidate has earned across all states — aka the "popular vote" — but rather by the number of "electoral votes" they've amassed by winning in individual states. With minor exceptions, the candidate who gets the most votes in a particular state on Election Day is awarded all of that state's electoral votes, which match the number of senators and representatives it sends to Congress. Whichever presidential ticket secures a majority of electoral votes — that is, 270 — wins. Due to the winner-take-all nature of the Electoral College, candidates tend not to campaign in states that consistently vote Democratic (blue states) or Republican (red states). Instead, they focus on the small number of states (known as swing states, battleground states, toss-up states or purple states) that could go one way or the other. The Founding Fathers established the Electoral College in the Constitution. Some of them wanted qualified citizens to elect the president by popular vote; others wanted Congress to elect the president. The Electoral College was the compromise they landed on. Today's Electoral College system evolved over time as individual states passed their own winner-take-all laws. But the Founders never specified how electors — the ones who cast the electoral votes — would be appointed. Instead, the Constitution explicitly delegates that power to the states themselves, saying they can choose their electors "in such Manner as the Legislature thereof may direct." National popular vote advocates argue that this clause gives state lawmakers " a built-in way to reform the system ." How could the national popular vote compact change America's presidential elections? Prior to the 20th century, three presidents won the White House without winning the popular vote: John Quincy Adams in 1824, Rutherford B. Hayes in 1876 and Benjamin Harrison in 1888. But the idea for a national popular vote compact only started to gain traction among scholars after George W. Bush lost the popular vote in 2000 and wound up in the White House anyway. Sixteen years later, Trump's popular-vote loss to Hillary Clinton — by a margin of nearly 3 million ballots — added more fuel to the fire. The Bush and Trump victories also polarized the issue, making Democrats more open to the idea of reform — and Republicans more opposed (in general). The NPVIC was introduced in 2006 by John Koza , a computer scientist and former Democratic elector who co-invented the lottery scratchcard. The idea is simple. First, individual states agree to award all of their electoral votes to the winner of the national popular vote. When enough states agree — that is, enough states with a combined total of at least 270 electoral votes — then the compact will take effect and the candidate who earns the most popular votes nationwide will be guaranteed enough electoral votes to win the White House. No constitutional amendment required. National popular vote proponents say that their plan will completely change the way candidates campaign for (and even govern as) president. Rather than lavishing all their time, energy and resources on a small handful of swing states, aspiring commanders in chief would in theory have to cater to voters everywhere in hopes of maximizing their nationwide vote tally. In April 2007, Maryland became the first state to sign on. Ten more jurisdictions followed suit before the 2016 election (California, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island, Vermont, Washington and the District of Columbia), with another eight joining the compact after Trump became president (Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Maine, Minnesota, New Mexico, Oregon and Virginia). Republican-led chambers have adopted the NPVIC in New York (2011), Oklahoma (2014) and Arizona (2016) — but generally, Democrats have needed complete statehouse control to enact it into law. Which is where Democrats' shiny new trifectas in Pennsylvania, Michigan, Arizona, Wisconsin and Nevada come into play. What's next According to the Times, "lawmakers in key states said on Thursday that they had already begun having conversations this week about introducing legislation to join the agreement in the next session, and were hopeful that they would succeed ahead of 2028." But hopeful doesn't mean certain. One of the new trifecta states, Michigan, failed to get over the line during its previous Democratic trifecta, from 2023 to 2024 — and Nevada fell short in 2019 when its then-Democratic governor vetoed the compact amid fears it could diminish his small state's outsized influence over presidential elections. Virginia became the most recent state to join the compact after Democrats there won a trifecta in 2025. Republicans called the move an " unconstitutional assault on our democracy ," arguing it undermines the influence of Virginia voters. One major question is whether lawmakers will prioritize the national popular vote after campaigning in 2026 on more visceral issues like lowering the cost of living. "Time will tell," Clinton Anderson, a Democratic state assemblyman in Wisconsin, told the Times. "I want to make it a priority, but it's not the thing I heard on the doors I knocked." Another question is what might happen in the courts if the compact actually kicks in. Notre Dame law professor Derek Muller has argued that the NPVIC would be unconstitutional without congressional approval — which, in his view, is required under the Constitution's Compact Clause. "It's a very real possibility that enough states join this compact," Muller told the Times. But, he added, "there will be a lot of challenges." On Tuesday, Americans voted overwhelmingly against data centers and artificial intelligence growth. In 40 of 41 local ballot races around the country, many in the state of Ohio, voters opted to restrict or prohibit new data center constructions in their areas. Much of the growing opposition to data centers has come from rising electricity prices , which are squeezing Americans in a time of already high prices and cost of living. But, according to a new study by researchers at Harvard University and the University of Pennsylvania, data centers are probably having only a small effect on residential electricity prices. The researchers calculated that these operations were responsible for just 4 percent of the utility rate increases over the last five years. Sign up for free “Even to me it was somewhat surprising,” said Serguei Netessine, professor at the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania and one of the study’s authors. In the run-up to the elections, Democrats pointed to data centers — and Republican support for their development — as key drivers of electricity price increases. In one campaign ad , Democrat James Talarico, now senator-elect of Texas, said that Texans were “paying the price with skyrocketing utility bills.” Sherrod Brown, Democratic senator-elect of Ohio, similarly argued that state residents were facing higher electricity bills due to the build-out of energy-hogging data centers. There are certainly some areas — like in Pennsylvania, Virginia, Ohio and other states covered by grid operator PJM — where data centers have skyrocketed demand, pushing some costs onto residential customers. But multiple studies by different researchers and organizations have failed to find a strong connection between data centers and the overall trajectory of U.S. electricity prices in recent years. Another analysis earlier this year by researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology found that, between 2010 and 2024, data centers increased average electricity prices for residential customers by just 2.1 percent. Last year, research from the Brattle Group and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory found that data centers were actually decreasing costs in certain regions. And another study by the Electric Power Research Institute found that a doubling of data center capacity between 2019 and 2024 resulted in a 4 percent drop in home electricity prices. For those customers, data centers were responsible for 15 percent of the price increase between 2020 and 2025. But for ordinary Americans, Netessine said, the changes simply were not substantial. “So far we have no evidence that data centers increase prices all that much,” Netessine said. Instead, he said, prices are rising due to more quotidian factors: rising gas prices, an aging electricity grid, and wildfires and hurricanes requiring improvements to the grid and recovery after disaster. Most of the cost of generating and delivering electricity is based on large, up-front capital costs, such as the costs to build power plants, wires and transmission lines to carry that power into homes. Some areas of the United States also have excess “capacity” in the grid — meaning that the grid is overbuilt for the actual demand. In those areas, adding a data center means that large fixed grid costs are spread over more consumers. That could lower prices. Of course, that’s not the case everywhere. PJM has had booming data center growth that has also required additional build-out of the power grid. This has raised prices at power capacity auctions, and states like Maryland have seen increasing residential prices that are at least in part from this boom. If the number of data centers continue to boom, experts say, residential prices could be affected more down the line. Data center electricity demand is expected to increase steeply over the next few years, requiring new power generation — wind, solar or natural gas — to be put onto the grid. And residents have issues with data centers that go beyond the price of electricity. The new developments have been singled out for loud noise , polluting power generation , and for disturbing residential neighborhoods and natural landscapes. According to the Pew Research Center, more than half of Americans say that data centers are mostly bad for the environment.
